I agree with most of your points (artificial general intelligence is very hard, although possible), but that's almost beside the basic issue... It will be narrow+ artificial intelligence (not specifically human=general, with all our faults and problems and hangups) that will make the breakthrough, because it will be much SMARTER, in all important ways, than mere humans can ever hope to be. The fact that robots will be created which act essentially like humans, but VASTLY smarter and wiser, will be within reach in about twenty five or thirty years -- while we are still alive. How we will DEAL with that is beyond my knowledge, because NOBODY knows. And any who tell you otherwise are fools.

This guy is starting to annoy me. This is almost a meme "you AI guys have it all wrong - listen to my brilliant idea, which has no empirical basis, and which I have not tested".

My suggestion is that he takes his amazing insights and builds an A(G)I using them. Until then, STFU.

A sufficient reason for the limited success of AI so far is that silicon computers are very weak computationally so far. When you look at the history of computers, software has consistently punched above its weight given the hardware resources available.

Arguably the brain has about 10^18 calculation cycles a second to play with, far in excess of even current supercomputers. (I revised my estimate up recently when I realised that there are maybe 100 latent synapses per active synapse and these latent synapses are being constantly updated as new data comes in).

He is a physicist and thus subject to Dunning Kruger syndrome when talking about computer science an philosophy. A bit like Roger Penrose's embarrassing speculations on the theory of mind.

His extolling of "Popperian epistemology" shows how out of date he is even philosophically.
